title: Quantization-Aware Training for Ultra-Low-Bit Reasoning LLMs
one_liner: A two-stage training pipeline that shrinks language models to 2-bit weights while keeping their reasoning ability intact by first stabilizing the network with mixed data, then fixing reasoning loss with a teacher.
lead: Language models are huge and expensive to run. Quantization (shrinking each number from 32 bits to 2 bits) makes them tiny, but it usually breaks their ability to reason through multi-step problems. This paper shows that the problem comes from how knowledge gets baked in during training, and fixes it with a two-step approach: first, stabilize the tiny weights using many kinds of data; second, use a trained teacher to fix the reasoning damage.

paras: Language models (trained neural networks that predict the next word) are so big they cost huge money to run. Quantization shrinks each stored number from 32 binary digits down to 2 digits, cutting memory and speed 16-fold. But when you shrink a network built to reason, something breaks: the model loses the ability to follow multi-step logic, solve math problems, or trace through complex ideas.

A beginner tries to just quantize after training is done (shrink the weights and hope). This fails because reasoning capability lives in subtle relationships between weights. Those relationships are fragile. Squeezing numbers into 2-bit bins destroys the delicate balance. The network can still spit out grammatical text, but it cannot think through problems anymore.

callout.html: Shrinking a reasoning model's numbers breaks the internal logic it learned.

steps.text: Quantize the model using examples from many domains (code, math, language) to learn which numbers matter most.
Fine-tune the 2-bit model using a full-size teacher that scores reasoning steps, steering it back toward correct logic.
Test on math and logic problems to verify the tiny model still solves them.
Show that this two-stage approach beats simpler methods by a huge margin.
Run the 2-bit model on cheap hardware while keeping reasoning intact.

paras: The paper changes the quantization process itself—the way numbers are squashed into 2-bit bins. Instead of a single rigid squashing rule, it uses a careful two-stage process: first with many data types to teach which weights matter, then with a teacher guiding the fine-tuning. The actual numbers stored in the network get reorganized to preserve the reasoning knowledge.

hidden.name: Reasoning preservation score
paras: This is not about whether the model gives any answer—it is about whether it gives the right answer to a problem that takes several steps to solve. A question like 'If Alice has 5 apples and Bob has 3 times as many, how many do they have together?' requires the model to track numbers, apply operations, and combine them correctly. This score measures: what fraction of multi-step reasoning problems does the 2-bit model still solve correctly? The paper estimates it by testing on math and logic benchmarks.

The paper measures this by running the quantized model on standard reasoning tests and comparing accuracy to the original full-size model. Mixed-domain calibration preserves this score better than single-domain calibration because it prevents the network from over-optimizing for one task and losing reasoning universality.

heat.caption: Darker means reasoning is preserved better during quantization.

reads.html: How much of the model's problem-solving ability survives when you shrink its numbers?
Accuracy on multi-step benchmarks (GSM8K, math word problems, logic puzzles) after 2-bit quantization.

paras: When you quantize a model all at once, every weight gets assigned a 2-bit value based on its size alone. Big weights get bigger 2-bit codes, small weights get smaller codes. But this global rule destroys the intricate relationships between weights that enable reasoning. A single-domain calibration (using only math examples, for instance) teaches the network to focus on math, and it forgets how to handle other domains.

The fix is two-stage. First stage: use calibration data from many domains (code, reasoning problems, general text, instruction-following). This teaches the quantization rule to be universal—it learns which weights matter across all types of knowledge, not just one type. The quantized network keeps the broad structure of reasoning intact. Second stage: take that quantized model and fine-tune it with a teacher. The teacher is a full-size model that sees a problem and rates how well the 2-bit model reasoned through it. The fine-tuning loss penalizes steps where the 2-bit model went wrong on reasoning, using the teacher's judgment as ground truth. This reward-based steering nudges the 2-bit weights back toward correct reasoning paths, repairing damage from quantization. Unlike a single-task approach that teaches the network to focus only on math or code, the mixed-domain method keeps the network's knowledge spread across all tasks.

stages.s: Collect calibration examples from multiple domains
Learn 2-bit quantization rule that preserves all-domain knowledge
Assign 2-bit weights using the calibrated rule
Run teacher model on reasoning tasks to generate rewards
Fine-tune 2-bit model using teacher rewards and reasoning loss

math.words: Quantization loss equals the standard training loss (how often the model gets the right answer) plus a penalty term that measures how far the quantized weights have drifted from the original weights, weighted by a calibration factor learned from mixed-domain data. Plus a teacher-guided reward term that pushes the model toward solutions the teacher rated as correct.
math.equation: L = L_base + lambda_q * C(theta_q, theta_orig) + lambda_r * L_teacher_reward
symbols: standard training loss (accuracy on the task)
strength of quantization penalty (how much to preserve original weights)
calibration-weighted distance between 2-bit weights and original weights
penalty for reasoning steps the teacher marked as wrong

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one weight is originally 3.7, and quantization places it at 2.0. The calibration says this weight is important (calibration factor 0.8).
Drift distance: (2.0 - 3.7) squared = 2.89. Weighted by calibration: 0.8 × 2.89 = 2.31.
Teacher says the reasoning step using this weight went slightly wrong (reward penalty 0.5).
L_base is 0.8 (some task accuracy loss). Lambda_q is 0.1, lambda_r is 0.2.
Adjusting this weight back toward 2.5 would reduce drift to 1.5 squared = 2.25, weighted = 1.8. Total drops to 1.1. Training nudges that direction.

math.note: The first penalty term keeps quantized weights close to the originals; the calibration factor learned from mixed domains tells the network which weights must stay precise. The teacher-reward term steers reasoning steps in the right direction.

charts.title: Post-training quantization (naive baseline)
charts.note: Shrinking the numbers breaks reasoning. Big drop because no guidance during compression.

charts.title: This paper: two-stage QAT
charts.note: Mixed-domain calibration and teacher guidance preserve reasoning. Only small drop from original.

items.html: If the mixed-domain calibration data does not include examples from the reasoning task you care about, the quantization rule will not adapt well. A model calibrated on code and general text but never math problems will struggle on math.
If the teacher model itself makes mistakes on reasoning, it will teach the 2-bit model to copy those mistakes. The teacher must be reliable.
If you fine-tune the 2-bit model too aggressively with the teacher, it may memorize the training reasoning steps and fail on new, unseen problems.

Use diverse calibration data, a high-quality teacher, and careful regularization to prevent over-fitting. Balance the two-stage process: enough calibration to preserve structure, enough teacher guidance to fix reasoning, but not so much that it memorizes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small reasoning model (about 100 million numbers to adjust during training), train it on a subset of math word problems. Split the test set in half. On the first half, quantize it naively (post-training quantization) and measure reasoning accuracy. On the second half, run the two-stage pipeline: calibrate with mixed examples (math, code, plain text) and then fine-tune with a full-size teacher. Show the accuracy gap. It should be dramatic: naive drops 40-50%, two-stage drops only 5-10%.
demo.closing: The two-stage pipeline nearly restores all reasoning ability even in a 2-bit model, while naive quantization destroys it. That difference is real and measurable.
